absent: Implementations and full error contracts of invoked but unrouted helpers for type checks, range checks, initialization predicates, per processor registration and teardown, and redistributor overlap beyond the distributor predicate shown.

Memory layouts and complete field sets for distributor state, interrupt descriptors, device and attribute containers, register region and I O device descriptors, and processor private interrupt state beyond observed members.
Contents and permissions of register tables for older and newer distributor, processor, redistributor and system register groups, plus behavior of system register and line level state helpers.

Guest memory access semantics, descriptor reference counting and table locking during the pending scan, and virtual machine virtual processor and doorbell lifecycle including direct interrupt availability.
Numeric values of fixed window spans, undefined address sentinel, processor identifier encodings, and exact bit positions of packed redistributor and line level fields beyond qualitative packing.
Allocation failure modes, teardown ordering beyond container release, and concurrency rules for indexed table iteration under the observed lock ordering.

findings.text: A single handler implements guest interrupt controller address setup and query for several address kinds. Caller supplied data is fetched from user memory on writes and on indexed region queries to obtain a selector; other reads return stored values to user memory only on success. Version specific kinds are validated against the created device flavor before any state is touched, and unrecognized kinds are rejected.

Placement contracts differ by generation. Older distributor and processor interface windows require 4 KiB alignment; newer distributor windows require 64 KiB alignment. Each kind has a fixed span consumed by range validation.

Legacy redistributor access uses the first configured region. A write with no selector establishes region zero with legacy semantics; a read reports an undefined sentinel when no region exists, otherwise the stored base of the leading region. Indexed region access packs selector, base, element count and flags into one caller value; writes demand a nonzero count with clear flags, reads reject unknown selectors and otherwise return selector combined with stored base and count.

Address handling serializes on the slots mutex slots_lock for its whole duration. Plain kinds then take the configuration mutex config_lock only around validation and update. Redistributor writes avoid nesting by delegating inner protection to the callee, which needs slots protection during later registration.

Redistributor region establishment is a two phase operation. Allocation and list insertion happen under configuration protection; per processor decode registration then runs without that protection but with slots protection held by the caller. If registration fails for any processor, the newly inserted region is located again under protection and released, so no partially registered region remains.

Bulk redistributor decode registration expects slots protection already held and walks every online processor in order, stopping at the first failure. On failure it walks back over predecessors and tears down what was installed in this attempt, returning the failure status; success returns cleanly with all processors covered.

Region allocation enforces ordering and compatibility. An empty table only accepts selector zero. A nonempty table only accepts the immediate successor of the current tail selector. Legacy unsized entries cannot be mixed with sized entries in either direction, and a second legacy entry is rejected. Candidates that wrap past the top of the address space, overlap any existing redistributor window, or in the legacy case intersect the distributor window, are rejected. Surviving candidates undergo range permission validation before insertion at the tail.

Each redistributor region record holds a guest base, an element count distinguishing legacy from sized entries, a selector, a cursor for the next free slot, and list linkage anchoring it in distributor order. Fresh records start from an undefined base, receive caller base and count only after validation, initialize the cursor to the beginning, and are then queued.
Distributor collision is a half open interval intersection test between a candidate window and the fixed size distributor window anchored at the stored distributor base.
Region lookup by selector performs a linear walk of the distributor region list and returns the first entry whose selector matches, or a null indicator when none matches.

Common device controls dispatch on group. Address controls delegate to the address handler with unknown subtypes remapped to a generic unknown control error. Interrupt count controls validate and install once. Control group supports initialization and pending table persistence, each with its own gating; anything else reports unknown control.

Total interrupt count must lie within a fixed window that reserves room for private interrupts plus a minimum of shared interrupts up to a defined maximum, and must be a multiple of the word width. Installation is guarded and single shot: if shared count is already nonzero the request is rejected as busy, otherwise the shared portion is derived by subtracting the private reservation.

Interrupt count installation and controller initialization both serialize on the configuration mutex. Pending table persistence additionally requires the newer generation flavor, then acquires the machine mutex, attempts to acquire all processor locks without waiting, and only then takes the configuration mutex; locks are released in reverse order. Contended processor locks abort the operation as busy without touching state.

Pending state persistence requires an initialized distributor. When host support for direct virtual interrupts is present, all virtual processors are detached before the scan and reattached afterwards even on failure. The scan walks the large interrupt table, skips entries that cannot be resolved or lack a target, caches guest reads by byte address, compares the guest stored bit against the software latch optionally refreshed from hardware for capable entries, and writes back only when they differ. The first guest access failure aborts the scan.

Detachment iterates over the bound virtual processor count and releases each per processor interrupt against its processor handle. Reattachment iterates the same way and issues a request per processor, flagging unexpected failures through a diagnostic check.

Direct virtual interrupt state is read from a per processor in memory table. Byte position derives from the interrupt identifier divided by bits per byte, bit position from the remainder; the reported value is the boolean presence of that bit.

Common queries mirror setup for address and interrupt count groups, with unknown address subtypes remapped the same way; interrupt count query returns shared plus private totals. Device creation delegates to the central creator with the caller type, and destruction only releases the device container.

Older generation register addressing splits the caller attribute into a processor selector and a masked offset. Processor resolution uses identifier lookup; failure to resolve is reported as invalid argument.

Older generation register access fetches the caller value before locking on writes. It then takes the machine mutex, attempts all processor locks without waiting, takes the configuration mutex, and ensures the controller is initialized before dispatching to processor interface or distributor helpers based on group. All locks release in reverse order; contended processors abort as busy, and successful reads copy the result back to caller memory.

Generation specific register helpers construct a transient descriptor naming the appropriate register table and its length, then delegate to a shared word access routine with direction, offset and value slot. The line level helper additionally requires a word aligned interrupt selector and routes writes and reads to dedicated line state helpers.

Shared word access separates read and write paths. Both resolve the target region for a word length; reads of unresolvable addresses report zero with success, writes to them report success without effect. When resolution succeeds, the access uses the redistributor bound processor if the descriptor carries one, otherwise the caller processor, preferring user access hooks when the region defines them and falling back to normal data path hooks.

Region resolution subtracts the device base from the access address, searches the descriptor tables, and validates the candidate. Validation maps access length to a width permission, requires the permission to be present and the address to be naturally aligned, accepts stateless regions immediately, and for per interrupt regions requires the decoded interrupt selector to be below the provisioned total.

Older generation dispatch routes distributor and processor register groups to the register path and everything else to common handling for both store and query. Existence probing accepts two address kinds, defers register groups to a register existence helper, accepts interrupt count queries, accepts only the initialization control, and rejects all else as unknown.

Older generation register existence first parses processor and offset, selects a register table by group with a zero base, rejects offsets that are not word aligned, and requires successful region resolution for a word length; any mismatch is reported as unknown.
Older generation operations record aggregates a human readable name with handlers for creation, destruction, store, query and existence probing.

Newer register addressing assumes the first processor for distributor registers and otherwise decodes affinity from the attribute, rebuilds a hardware processor identifier from four affinity levels, and resolves it; unresolvable processors are invalid, and the offset is always the masked low portion.

Newer generation register access distinguishes system register controls, which bypass generic caller copying, from other groups which copy a word on writes before locking. After acquiring machine, all processor and configuration protection in the same order as the older path, it requires either an initialized controller or one of two allowlisted distributor identification registers; otherwise it reports busy. It then dispatches to distributor, redistributor, system register, or line level handlers, with line level demanding a specific info selector and masking an interrupt selector. Successful generic reads copy back to caller memory.
Interrupt count ABI facts: minimum total accounts for private interrupts plus 32 shared; maximum total is 1024; granularity is 32.

Indexed redistributor ABI packs four fields into one 64 bit caller value: a low selector, a masked base, a count field and a flags field. Writes interpret base through a base mask and count and flags through dedicated masks; reads return selector plus stored base plus stored count shifted into the count position.
The allowlisted pre-initialization registers are GICD_IIDR and GICD_TYPER2; all other register groups require an initialized controller.

Address kinds distinguish older distributor, older processor interface, newer distributor, newer legacy redistributor and newer indexed region. Common groups distinguish address, interrupt count and control; older register groups add distributor and processor registers; newer register groups add distributor, redistributor, system registers and line level info.

Caller memory accesses can fail; fetch failures on writes and indexed queries abort before locking side effects beyond the fetch, and store back failures on successful reads are reported as the final status.

Concurrent access hazards are contained by nonblocking acquisition of all processor locks, with busy reported without partial updates, and by unwinding partially installed redistributor decode and discarding the freshly allocated region when bulk registration fails.
